claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and distribution of nanoscale, chemically segregated grain-boundary regions.
Slower cooling after solution treatment causes nanoscale, chemically segregated grain-boundary regions to develop.
Nanoscale, chemically segregated grain-boundary regions impede crack initiation and propagation.
Rapid quenching from solution treatment produces a largely homogeneous, metastable microstructure in the proposed equiatomic alloy.
Slower cooling promotes solute migration and controlled segregation at grain boundaries.
The relevant structural mediator comprises grain-boundary local chemical ordering and a nanoscale, chemically segregated phase distribution.
Slower cooling provides sufficient time for solute atoms to diffuse to and segregate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation forms a thin, enriched film.
The thin, enriched grain-boundary film hinders crack initiation.
The thin, enriched grain-boundary film restricts crack propagation.
Rapid quenching retains a homogeneous microstructure that lacks the proposed beneficial grain-boundary features.
A rapidly quenched homogeneous microstructure is more prone to embrittlement under demanding service conditions.
The slower-cooled alloy will have higher fracture toughness or impact energy than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The proposed behavior applies only where diffusion is sufficient for controlled segregation but insufficient to form large, brittle secondary phases.
Extensive diffusion can produce large, brittle secondary phases.
The magnitude of toughness improvement may vary with alloy chemistry and processing parameters.
Failure of slower-cooled samples to show a statistically significant toughness or impact-energy increase relative to the quenched control is specified as a falsifying outcome.
Failure to observe increased grain-boundary segregation after slower cooling is specified as a falsifying outcome.
